The PhD program in Mechanical Engineering at The Catholic University of America combines rigorous advanced coursework with innovative, faculty-guided research in a flexible and supportive academic environment. Through close mentorship and access to research opportunities in Washington, DC, doctoral students develop the technical expertise and research experience necessary for leadership careers in academia, industry, and government laboratories.

At a Glance
Flexible Doctoral Study: The PhD program may be completed on either a full-time or part-time basis and requires 53 credit hours beyond a STEM undergraduate degree, including advanced coursework, two engineering mathematics classes, a comprehensive exam, and a doctoral dissertation.
Diverse Research Opportunities: Students can pursue advanced research in biomaterials, robotics, acoustics and vibrations, energy storage, composites, carbon nanotubes, manufacturing, and other emerging engineering fields.
Close Faculty Mentorship: Small class sizes and individualized advising allow doctoral students to work closely with faculty members on cutting-edge research projects and professional development.
Access to Washington, DC Resources: The university’s location provides opportunities for collaboration with federal laboratories, government agencies, research institutions, and engineering companies throughout the Washington metropolitan area.
Program Details
The PhD program in Mechanical Engineering at The Catholic University of America provides students with advanced technical education and intensive research experience within a collaborative, highly personalized academic environment. The program is designed for students pursuing careers in research, higher education, government laboratories, or advanced engineering leadership. Students may complete the degree on either a full-time or part-time basis, allowing flexibility for both traditional doctoral students and working professionals.
Specializations in Research
A major strength of the program is the diversity of research opportunities available to doctoral students. Faculty research spans a broad range of modern engineering disciplines, allowing students to engage in both fundamental and applied research with real-world impact.
In biomaterials and biomedical engineering, Dr. Santiago Solares and Dr. Xiaolong Luo conduct research involving biomaterials, biofabrication, advanced characterization methods, and biomedical applications of engineered materials. Their work combines mechanical engineering, materials science, and biology to address challenges related to medical devices and advanced manufacturing technologies.
Research in robotics and intelligent systems is led by Dr. Zhaoyang Wang and Dr. Jeffrey Herrmann. Their research includes robotics, automation, control systems, metareasoning and decision, and intelligent engineering processes. Students working in these areas gain experience in both theoretical and applied aspects of robotics and autonomous systems.
Catholic University also has a long-standing reputation in acoustics and vibrations. Dr. Joseph Vignola and Dr. Diego Turo conduct research in structural vibrations, atmospheric sound propagation, machinery noise control, and laser based technics for art conservation. Students participate in analytical, computational, and experimental research projects relevant to both industry and government applications.
In energy systems research, Dr. Chuan-Fu Lin leads work involving batteries, energy storage technologies, and advanced thermal systems. Dr. Jandro Abot conducts research in composite materials and carbon nanotube technologies with applications in aerospace and advanced structural systems.
Benefits
Graduate students benefit from small class sizes, close faculty mentorship, and access to research opportunities throughout the Washington, DC area, including collaborations with federal agencies, laboratories, and private industry. Graduates leave prepared to make significant contributions in academia, industry, and government through advanced research, innovation, and engineering leadership.
Curriculum
The PhD curriculum in Mechanical Engineering within the The Catholic University of America’s College of Engineering, Physics, and Computing is designed to provide students with both advanced technical depth and the flexibility to support individualized research goals. The program requires a minimum of 53 credit hours beyond a STEM undergraduate degree, including two graduate-level engineering mathematics courses that provide strong analytical and computational foundations for advanced research.
Students work closely with their faculty advisor to select graduate courses that align with their area of specialization and dissertation topic. Coursework may include advanced subjects in mechanical engineering as well as interdisciplinary courses from related fields, allowing students to develop the technical expertise necessary for original research and professional leadership.
